title: Land Still to Take, Land Already Given
sum: Joshua is old, and God tells him that much land remains: the Philistine coast, the Phoenician north, Lebanon to Lebo-hamath. Yet he is to hand it out by lot now, trusting God to drive out its people. Before the lots are cast west of the Jordan, the chapter records what Moses gave east of it: Reuben's high plain north of the Arnon, Gad's half of Gilead, and the eastern half of Manasseh in Bashan.

Twice the chapter says that Levi received no land, because the LORD and his offerings are its inheritance (13:14, 33). The note that Israel did not drive out Geshur and Maacah (13:13) is the first of several such admissions in this half of the book.
readings: Read as a map of promise

The chapter starts with what is not yet Israel's and divides it anyway. The map is drawn on God's word, not on Israel's control. Readers see faith, and also a warning: what is promised still has to be taken up.
Read as a record of the east
For the two and a half tribes, the chapter is a deed of title. It lists towns that turn up again in the Mesha Stele of Moab, a reminder that these lands were long contested.

views.H: A record of Joshua's last years and of Moses' grants east of the Jordan. The "land that remains" was a real list of unconquered regions, partly taken under David.
views.C: Most critical scholars see 13:2–6 as an ideal map like Numbers 34, and the eastern lists as drawn from administrative records of the monarchy. The tension with 11:23 shows the book combining a sweeping and a gradual view of conquest.
views.E: The chapter shows that the conquest was partial. Those who wrestle with the ban note that the book's own maps include peoples who were never destroyed and lived on beside Israel (13:13).
views.J: The rabbis read the division of the land as Joshua's last great task. The Talmud says the land was divided by lot and by the Urim and Thummim together (Bava Batra 122a). Maimonides wrote that anyone who devotes himself to serving God may be counted like the tribe of Levi, with the LORD as his portion.
views.X: Christian writers from Origen on read the land shares as a picture of the spiritual inheritance of believers (Ephesians 1:11–14; 1 Peter 1:4). Levi's portion, God himself, became a picture of those who give up earthly security for God.

deep.h: The Mesha Stele and the eastern towns
deep.b: Found at Dhiban (Dibon) in 1868, the stone of Mesha king of Moab (about 840 BC) tells how Mesha threw off the rule of Israel's King Omri and his son. It names many towns in this chapter: Medeba, Dibon, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim, Jahaz, Aroer and Bezer. It also says "the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old." So a Moabite king confirms that Gad was settled east of the Jordan, while also showing that Reuben's land changed hands. Compare 2 Kings 3:4–27.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the order of the lists tells a story
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The book opens the land division with what Israel has not taken (13:1–6) and then with what Moses gave (13:8–33), before Joshua gives anything. The effect is to set Joshua's distribution between two kinds of inheritance: one already given by Moses and one still promised by God. Joshua's own share comes only at the end (19:49–50). The structure seems to make the point that the land is never simply won; it is received, first from Moses, then from God's future action. Commentators such as Hawk and Nelson note the frame of Caleb and Joshua; I am extending that observation to the chapter's opening.

echoes: Numbers 32:1–42; Numbers 34:1–15; Deuteronomy 3:8–17; Deuteronomy 18:1–2; Judges 3:1–4; 2 Kings 3:4–27; Psalm 16:5–6

settings.what: Land still to be taken, and the command to divide it
settings.why: God lists the land still not taken, the Philistine coast and the north, and promises to drive out its people. Joshua must divide the land by lot now. Later readers knew Philistines and Phoenicians on their borders. For them, the speech explains that the promise was larger than what Israel held.

title: Caleb at Eighty-Five
sum: The division west of the Jordan begins. Eleazar, Joshua and the family heads give out the land by lot, as Moses commanded, for nine and a half tribes. Levi gets towns, not land, and Joseph counts as two tribes.

Then Caleb steps forward. Forty-five years earlier he and Joshua alone had trusted God at Kadesh. Now at 85 he is as strong as ever, and he asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the giant Anakim had fortified towns. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron, which stays his family's "to this day" because he followed the LORD fully.
readings: Read as a portrait of faith

Caleb's story is the heart of the land chapters. He asks not for easy land but for the very place that frightened Israel forty-five years before. Three times the chapter says he "followed the LORD fully."
Read as an outsider made insider
Caleb is a Kenizzite, from a clan with Edomite ties. The man who best models Israel's faith may have been born outside Israel, a pattern the book also shows in Rahab.

views.H: Caleb's numbers (40 at Kadesh, 85 now) fix the conquest at about seven years, as Jewish chronology also counts it.
views.C: Many scholars see Caleb as a southern clan hero whose clan held Hebron, absorbed into Judah's story. The tradition that Caleb, not Joshua, took Hebron (15:13–19; Judges 1:10–20) sits beside 10:36–37 and 11:21–22.
views.E: Caleb's request is for land held by others, and the book frames it as faith. Readers concerned with ethics note that the request presupposes driving people out, though in this case the people are the feared Anakim of Israel's memory.
views.J: Caleb is a model of the righteous man in rabbinic tradition. The Talmud says that during the spying he went alone to pray at the patriarchs' graves in Hebron (Bavli Sotah 34b); now Hebron becomes his.
views.X: Christian preachers make Caleb a picture of lifelong faithfulness and of courage in old age. Hebrews 3–4 uses the Kadesh story as a warning against unbelief, and Caleb is the counterexample.

echoes: Numbers 13:6; Numbers 13:30; Numbers 14:6–9; Numbers 14:24; Numbers 32:12; Deuteronomy 1:36; Judges 1:10–20; Hebrews 3:16–19

settings.by: Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite
settings.to: Joshua, with the people of Judah at Gilgal
settings.when: as the land west of the Jordan is divided
settings.why: At 85, Caleb reminds Joshua of Moses' promise at Kadesh, when only the two of them trusted God. He asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the giant Anakim lived. The speech contrasts the faith of one old man of the first generation with the fear that kept his whole generation out. Caleb, a Kenizzite by clan, is held up as a model for all Israel.

title: Judah's Borders and Towns
sum: Judah receives the first and largest share. Its borders are traced in detail: the south line repeats Moses' southern border, the east is the Dead Sea, the north runs up past the Valley of Achor and along the south side of Jerusalem, and the west is the Mediterranean. In the middle Caleb takes Hebron, offers his daughter Achsah to whoever captures Debir, and she wins springs of water for her land.

Then come about 115 towns in four regions, the Negev, the Shephelah, the hill country and the wilderness, grouped in districts. The chapter ends with a frank note: Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem.
readings: Read as a map

Many of these towns can be found today. Read with a map, the list shows the real geography of Judah: desert towns in the south, the foothill cities that guarded the passes, the hill towns around Hebron and Bethlehem, and a few outposts by the Dead Sea.
Read as a story within a list

In the middle of the borders and lists sits a family story: an old warrior, a bold younger man, and a daughter who asks her father for water and gets twice what she asked. Lists and stories work together in Joshua.

views.H: The district list records Joshua's allotment, with later updates as towns grew. The "to this day" of 15:63 points to a source written before David took Jerusalem.
views.C: Scholars date the district list to Judah's monarchy: Jehoshaphat (Cross and Wright), Hezekiah, or Josiah (Alt). Its twelve districts look like royal administration.
views.E: The Achsah story raises questions about a daughter offered as a prize. Many readers note that the text gives her the decisive voice.
views.J: The rabbis linked Othniel with learning: the Talmud says he restored laws forgotten in the mourning for Moses (Bavli Temurah 16a). Kiriath-arba was read as "town of the four" couples buried there.
views.X: Christian readers note that Judah's list in the Hebrew lacks Bethlehem, the town of David and of Jesus' birth; the Greek district restores it (see the variant at 15:59). Gehenna, Jesus' word for judgment, begins here as a boundary valley (15:8).

deep.b: The list moves through Judah's four natural zones. The Negev (15:21–32) is the dry south around Beersheba and Arad. The Shephelah (15:33–47) is the band of low hills facing the coast, with fortress towns like Lachish, Azekah and Mareshah, and the Philistine plain beyond. The hill country (15:48–60) is the ridge from Hebron north toward Jerusalem. The wilderness (15:61–62) is the dry slope down to the Dead Sea. Within these, eleven groups of towns end with a total, and the Greek adds a twelfth group (15:59). Many scholars think these were tax or military districts under Judah's kings.

echoes: Numbers 34:3–6; Judges 1:9–20; Judges 3:9–11; Nehemiah 11:25–30; 1 Chronicles 4:28–33; 2 Samuel 5:6–9; Hosea 2:15; Mark 9:43–48

settings.what: Achsah asks for pools of water
settings.when: when she comes to her husband Othniel
settings.why: Achsah asks for a blessing: pools of water for her dry land in the Negev, and she gets the upper and lower pools. Her bold request shows a woman securing her family's future, and the story is told again in Judges 1:12–15.

title: Joseph's Lot: Ephraim
sum: The descendants of Joseph receive the central hill country. The chapter traces their southern border from Jericho up past Bethel to Beth-horon and Gezer, then Ephraim's own border, with Michmethath, Taanath-shiloh and the Kanah Valley.
Ephraim also holds towns inside Manasseh's land. The chapter ends with the first of the northern failures: the Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but made to do forced labor, "to this day."
readings: Read as geography
Ephraim's hills were the most fertile and defensible part of the central highlands. Later this tribe gave its name to the whole northern kingdom.
Read as a moral note
The short closing verse matters: Gezer was spared and put to work. The book reports it without comment, but Judges will make such half-measures the root of Israel's troubles.

views.H: Gezer remained Canaanite until a pharaoh destroyed it and gave it to Solomon (1 Kings 9:16), as both the Bible and archaeology attest.
views.C: The border descriptions are often taken as some of the oldest material in the land chapters, perhaps from the time of the judges. The note on forced labor may reflect Solomon's day.
views.E: Forced labor instead of the ban shows coexistence in practice. It also shows another kind of injustice: conquered people as an unpaid work force.
views.J: Joshua himself was of Ephraim. Jewish tradition saw in Ephraim's pride (Judges 8; 12) the seeds of the later split of the kingdom under Jeroboam, an Ephraimite.
views.X: Little Christian comment attaches to this chapter. Origen's Homilies on Joshua read the incomplete conquest as the soul's unfinished struggle with sin: some "Canaanites" remain to be overcome.

title: Manasseh, Five Daughters, and a Forest
sum: Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, already has Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan through Machir. West of the river ten shares go to Manasseh's clans, five of them to the daughters of Zelophehad, who remind Eleazar and Joshua of the LORD's command through Moses. Manasseh's border with Ephraim is tangled, and it holds towns in the great valleys, Beth-shean, Megiddo, Taanach, but cannot drive out their Canaanites.

The house of Joseph then complains that one lot is too little for so great a people. Joshua tells them to clear the forest of the hill country, and promises they will overcome even the Canaanites' iron chariots.
readings: Read as justice for women

The daughters' case, settled in Numbers 27 and 36, is carried out here. Their shares count fully among the ten portions. The chapter shows the law working, but only because the women came forward again.
Read as pioneering
Joshua's answer to Joseph is practical: clear the forest. Archaeology shows exactly this, new hill villages with terraces and cisterns, as Israel took root in the highlands.

views.H: The clan names match district names on the Samaria ostraca, confirming that these were real families of Manasseh.
views.C: Scholars see the clan list as genealogy made from place names. The valley cities that Manasseh could not take were Canaanite and Egyptian strongholds into the 1100s BC, which fits archaeology.
views.E: Iron chariots in the valleys, forced labor in 17:13: the chapter is honest that Israel lived alongside the Canaanites and sometimes ruled them harshly.
views.J: The rabbis praised Zelophehad's daughters as wise and righteous (Bava Batra 119b). Their story is read on the Sabbath of Pinchas and cited in discussions of women and inheritance.
views.X: Christian readers have used the daughters as an example of bold, persistent prayer that claims God's promises. Megiddo, named here, becomes Revelation's Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).

echoes: Numbers 26:29–34; Numbers 27:1–11; Numbers 36:1–12; Judges 1:27–28; Judges 4:3; 1 Chronicles 7:14–19

settings.what: The daughters of Zelophehad claim their share
settings.by: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah
settings.to: Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the leaders
settings.when: during the division of Manasseh's land
settings.why: The five daughters remind the leaders of the LORD's command through Moses (Numbers 27:1–11). They are to receive land among their father's brothers. They get it. The scene shows the law of Moses being kept in the division, and a family without sons keeping its land.

settings.by: The house of Joseph, and Joshua in reply
settings.why: The descendants of Joseph complain that one share is too small for so great a people. They fear the Canaanites' iron chariots in the valleys. Joshua tells them to clear the forest of the hill country. He promises, "You will drive out the Canaanites, even though they have iron chariots" (17:18). For later readers, the reply honors the great northern tribes. It also shows them too timid to take what was given.

title: The Survey from Shiloh
sum: Israel moves its center to Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting; the land lies subdued. Seven tribes still have no land. Joshua rebukes their slowness and sends three men from each tribe to walk the land and write it up in seven parts. He casts lots before the LORD.

Benjamin's lot falls between Judah and Joseph: a narrow strip from the Jordan up through Bethel and Gibeon to the edge of Jerusalem. Its border runs along Judah's in reverse, and its towns include Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, Mizpeh, Gibeah and Jerusalem.
readings: Read as a new beginning
The tent at Shiloh in a subdued land echoes creation (Genesis 1:28) and the building of the tabernacle. Worship takes its place at the center before the rest of the land is divided.
Read as a call to action
"How long will you hang back?" The land is given but not yet taken up. The survey is a practical step: a written description so that the shares can be fair.

views.H: Shiloh served as Israel's central sanctuary from Joshua to Eli. Its destruction around 1050 BC fits the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4.
views.C: Many critical scholars see the Shiloh setting and the survey as later framing for older border lists; Benjamin's lists may come from the monarchy. Some see a priestly writer's hand in 18:1.
views.E: The survey implies fairness among tribes: land is described and valued before it is assigned. That fairness among Israel's tribes stands beside the loss suffered by the land's earlier people.
views.J: The Talmud says the tabernacle stood at Shiloh 369 years (Zevachim 118b) and that sacrifices could be eaten anywhere in sight of Shiloh. Benjamin, with Jerusalem on its border, was later honored as the tribe in whose land the temple stood (Deuteronomy 33:12).
views.X: Christian readers have noted Benjamin's line through Saul to Paul (Philippians 3:5), and Jesus' warning to the temple echoes Jeremiah's use of Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12–14; Mark 11:17).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the survey as a second spy mission
deep.b: This is my own reading. In Numbers 13 twelve men, one per tribe, went through the land and came back with a report that made Israel's heart melt. Here twenty-one men, three per tribe, survey the land and bring back a written description that leads to the land being divided. The two stories share a verb: the scouts spoke of "the land we passed through to scout out" (Numbers 13:32; 14:7), and the surveyors "passed through the land" (18:9). Joshua's order to "walk through the land" (18:4, 8) recalls another scene, when God told Abram, "Get up and walk through the land, its length and its width, for I will give it to you" (Genesis 13:17). Joshua and Caleb are the two survivors of the first mission. I suggest the writer means the survey to undo the failed mission of Kadesh, with Abraham's walk in the background: men again pass through the land, and this time their report leads to taking it. I have not seen this argued at length, though commentators note the link of Caleb's story (14:6–15) with Numbers 13–14.

echoes: Genesis 1:28; Numbers 13:17–33; Judges 18:31; 1 Samuel 1:3; Psalm 78:60; Jeremiah 7:12–14; Deuteronomy 33:12

settings.to: The Israelites gathered at Shiloh, especially the seven tribes without land
settings.when: after the tent of meeting is set up at Shiloh
settings.why: Joshua asks how long they will hang back from taking the land. He sends three men from each tribe to survey it and write it up in seven parts. He will cast lots before the LORD. The speech pushes a settled people to finish the task.

title: Six Lots, and Joshua's Own
sum: The remaining six tribes receive their lots: Simeon inside Judah, then the four Galilee tribes Zebulun, Issachar, Asher and Naphtali, and finally Dan on the coastal plain. Dan loses its land and moves north to capture Leshem, renaming it Dan.

When all the tribes have their shares, the Israelites give Joshua the town he asks for, Timnath-serah in Ephraim's hills. The division ends at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
readings: Read as the tribes' map

This chapter fixes the places that later stories assume: Samson's Zorah, Jonah's Gath-hepher, Tabor, Shunem, Jezreel, Kedesh, Hazor, Tyre and Sidon at Asher's edge, and the Galilee where Jesus would preach.
Read as leadership
The leader takes his share last. Caleb asked first and received the hardest land; Joshua asks last and receives a small hill town. The two faithful spies frame the whole division.

views.H: The lists record real tribal holdings. Simeon's list dates from before David (1 Chronicles 4:31), and Dan's move north is told in Judges 18.
views.C: Galilee's lists are thinner and many scholars think they are partly built from border points. The note on Dan anticipates Judges 18 and may be added from it.
views.E: Dan's conquest of quiet Laish (Judges 18:27–28) is told in Judges as an unprovoked attack. Joshua's single sentence passes over what Judges presents in a troubling light.
views.J: Jewish tradition preserved Timnath-heres, "portion of the sun," as a memorial of the day the sun stood still for Joshua (Rashi on Judges 2:9). Zebulun and Issachar were paired as merchant and scholar, the one supporting the other's study of Torah (from Deuteronomy 33:18–19).
views.X: Matthew 4:13–16 quotes Isaiah 9:1–2 on "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali": the tribes allotted Galilee here are where Jesus' ministry begins.

echoes: Genesis 49:5–21; Deuteronomy 33:18–25; Judges 1:30–35; Judges 18:1–31; Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:13–16; 1 Chronicles 4:24–33

title: Six Cities of Refuge
sum: God tells Joshua to appoint the cities of refuge commanded through Moses. A person who killed someone by accident may run to one, tell his case to the elders at the gate, and live there safe from the avenger of blood until he stands trial and until the high priest dies. Then he may go home.
Israel sets apart Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in Ephraim and Hebron in Judah, and east of the Jordan Bezer, Ramoth-gilead and Golan. The protection covers foreigners living in Israel as well.
readings: Read as law in the land
With the land divided, Israel's justice system takes physical form. Six towns turn the principle of Exodus 21:13 into places on the map, spaced so no one is too far from safety.
Read as grace
Christian readers have long seen the cities as pictures of refuge in God or in Christ (Psalm 46:1; Hebrews 6:18). Jewish teaching saw in them the balance of mercy and justice.

views.H: The cities were established as Moses ordered and functioned within Israel's legal order, though no narrative shows one in use.
views.C: The chapter blends wording from Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19. The shorter Greek text lacks most of the Deuteronomy language, which many scholars take as evidence of later expansion. The system itself may have grown out of altar asylum.
views.E: The law limits blood vengeance: intent matters, the accused gets a hearing, and foreigners are protected. It is one of the Bible's clearest steps from private revenge toward public justice.
views.J: Tractate Makkot sets out the rules: roads kept open with signs reading "Refuge," two scholars to accompany the fugitive, and the cities to have markets and water so no one would suffer for lack of them.
views.X: Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers "who have fled for refuge." Church fathers and Puritan preachers drew out the picture of Christ as the city, and the high priest's death as setting the guilty free.

echoes: Exodus 21:12–14; Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 4:41–43; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; 1 Kings 1:50–53; Hebrews 6:18

settings.what: The law of the towns of refuge
settings.to: The Israelites, the elders at each town gate, and anyone who kills by accident, including the foreigner living among them
settings.why: God tells Joshua to appoint the towns of refuge commanded through Moses. A person who killed by accident may flee and state his case to the elders at the gate. He stays safe from the avenger of blood until he stands trial, and until the high priest dies. The law, from Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19, now takes effect in the land, at six named towns.

title: Forty-Eight Towns for Levi
sum: The Levite family heads remind the leaders of Moses' command, and Israel gives them forty-eight towns with pastureland, by lot. Aaron's priests receive thirteen towns in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin; the other Kohathites ten in Ephraim, Dan and western Manasseh; the Gershonites thirteen in the north and in Bashan; the Merarites twelve in Zebulun and east of the Jordan. All six cities of refuge are among them.

The chapter, and the whole division of the land, ends with a summary of fulfillment: the LORD gave Israel all the land he had sworn, gave them rest on every side, and not one of his good words fell short.
readings: Read as the Levites among the tribes
Levi has no territory, but its towns are spread through every tribe. Teachers of the law and keepers of worship live everywhere in Israel, not just at the sanctuary.
Read as the book's turning point
21:43–45 is the theological summit of Joshua. After chapters of borders, towns and admissions of failure, the narrator steps back and declares God faithful.

views.H: The list carries out Numbers 35:1–8. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 6:54–81 shows it was preserved and copied.
views.C: The list is dated variously: to David and Solomon (Albright, Mazar), to Josiah, or after the exile (A. Graeme Auld, who argued that it grew out of the shorter list in 1 Chronicles 6). The summary in 21:43–45 is widely seen as the Deuteronomistic writer's voice.
views.E: The summary claims all enemies were handed over. Ethical readers note the gap between this triumphant language and the book's own record of peoples who remained, and ask how much is rhetoric.
views.J: Jewish tradition values the Levites' scattering as a blessing: teachers of Torah were placed throughout the land (compare Deuteronomy 33:10). Solomon quotes the promise of 21:45 at the temple (1 Kings 8:56).
views.X: Hebrews 4:8 reads 21:44 in light of Psalm 95: "If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day." The rest of the land points ahead to a Sabbath rest still open to God's people.

echoes: Numbers 35:1–8; 1 Chronicles 6:54–81; Deuteronomy 12:9–10; 1 Kings 8:56; Psalm 95:11; Hebrews 4:1–11

settings.by: The family heads of the Levites
settings.to: Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the heads of the tribes, at Shiloh
settings.when: after the tribes receive their land
settings.why: The Levites remind the leaders of the LORD's command through Moses: they must be given towns with pastures (Numbers 35:1–8). Israel does so. The scene shows the people keeping the law even when it costs each tribe some of its land.

traditions.q: Was God's promise of the land fully kept, or is it still waiting for Israel?
views: The promise was kept, as 21:43–45 says, and in Christ it widens to the whole earth that God's people will inherit (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16). Covenant theologians such as O. Palmer Robertson do not see the modern State of Israel as a fulfillment of the land promise.

Israel held the land only in part and later lost it, so the full promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) still waits for a future kingdom in which Israel lives securely in all its land (Charles Ryrie; John Walvoord). Many see the return of Jews to the land since 1948 as a step toward it.

God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable, 2015). But the Church does not read the modern State of Israel as fulfilling a promise of Scripture; it treats it under the common principles of international law (Notes, 1985).

The fathers read the land as a figure of the kingdom of heaven, the true inheritance. The Orthodox Church teaches no future return to the land as a fulfillment of prophecy, and many Orthodox Christians in the Holy Land, most of them Palestinian Arabs, reject Christian Zionism.

title: The Altar by the Jordan
sum: Joshua sends the eastern tribes home with praise, blessing and plunder, and with a charge in the language of Deuteronomy: love the LORD, hold on to him, serve him with all your heart. On the way they build a huge altar by the Jordan. The other tribes hear of it and gather at Shiloh for war.

Phinehas the priest and ten leaders go first to ask. They recall the sin of Peor and Achan's theft, and offer to share their own land if the eastern land is unclean. The eastern tribes swear by God's triple name that the altar is not for sacrifice but a copy, a witness that they too have a share in the LORD. Phinehas is satisfied, Israel praises God, and the altar is named as a witness that the LORD is God.
readings: Read as a story of unity
The chapter is a near civil war averted by talking first. Both sides act from loyalty to God: one fears a rival altar, the other fears being cut off from Israel's worship.
Read as a story about one altar
The whole crisis assumes that sacrifice belongs at one altar only (Deuteronomy 12). The eastern tribes' defense works because they accept that rule.

views.H: An event at the end of the conquest, before the elders who served with Joshua died. Phinehas's role fits his place in Numbers 25 and 31 and Judges 20.
views.C: Many scholars see a late story, written in priestly language to defend the single sanctuary and to affirm that Israelites east of the Jordan are true Israel. Some suspect an older memory of a real altar at the Jordan behind it.
views.E: The story is a model of conflict resolution: accusation, inquiry, explanation, acceptance. It contrasts with Judges 20, where Israel goes to war against Benjamin with terrible cost.
views.J: Jewish teachers have used the chapter to teach judging others favorably and the need to investigate before acting.
views.X: Preachers apply the story to divisions among Christians: speak first, assume good faith, and recognize that different expressions can share one loyalty (Ephesians 4:1–6).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the altar as the eastern tribes' Gilgal stones
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. In chapter 4 Israel set up twelve stones at Gilgal so that when "your children ask in time to come, 'What do these stones mean?'" the parents could tell the story (4:6–7, 21–22). The eastern tribes use almost the same scene: "In days to come your children may say to ours" (22:24; compare 22:27–28). The words gelilot (22:10) and gilgal share a root. I suggest the altar is meant as the eastern tribes' own memorial of the crossing, built because the twelve stones at Gilgal stood on the other side of the river. This overlaps with scholars who note the "children's question" form in both passages, but the direct pairing is my proposal.

echoes: Numbers 25:1–13; Numbers 32:1–32; Deuteronomy 12:5–14; Deuteronomy 13:12–18; Judges 20:1–48; Isaiah 19:19–20; Genesis 31:44–52

settings.what: Joshua sends the eastern tribes home
settings.to: The fighting men of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh
settings.when: after the wars, when the land has rest
settings.why: Joshua praises them for keeping their promise, blesses them, and sends them home with great wealth. He charges them in the words of Deuteronomy (22:5). They must love the LORD, walk in his ways, hold on to him, and serve him with all their heart. The river now separates them from the other tribes, and the charge is meant to keep them in the covenant.

settings.by: Phinehas and ten leaders; the eastern tribes in reply
settings.to: The tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh in Gilead, and through them the whole community gathered at Shiloh
settings.when: when the eastern tribes build a large altar by the Jordan
settings.why: The western tribes fear the altar is rebellion against the one place of worship. They recall the sin of Peor and Achan's theft. The eastern tribes swear by God's triple name that it is only a copy. It is a witness that they too belong to the LORD. War is avoided. For later readers, the story upholds one altar and also warns against cutting off fellow Israelites across the river.
views: Many critical scholars read the story as written to support the law of one place of worship (Deuteronomy 12) and the unity of all Israel.
Others see priestly language and concerns, from the time of the Second Temple, when Jews lived in many lands. Nelson and Butler both discuss the priestly features of the story.

title: Joshua's Warning
sum: Old and near death, Joshua calls Israel's leaders together. God has fought for them; the nations that remain will be driven out too if Israel holds to the law of Moses. Joshua warns them not to speak the names of the nations' gods, not to marry them, and not to let go of the LORD.

Every good word God spoke has come true. Just as surely, Joshua warns, every bad word will come true if they break the covenant: the remaining nations will become traps, lashes and thorns, and Israel will vanish from the good land.
readings: Read as a farewell sermon
Like Moses in Deuteronomy and Samuel in 1 Samuel 12, Joshua gives a last address. Its themes are memory, loyalty, and the two-sided faithfulness of God.
Read from exile
For readers who lived after 586 BC, when Judah lost the land, the warning reads as an explanation of what happened. The good land was lost exactly as Joshua said it could be.

views.H: Joshua's actual farewell to Israel's leaders, years after the conquest.
views.C: A classic Deuteronomistic speech, one of the key passages Martin Noth used to identify the Deuteronomistic History. Its warnings of losing the land suggest a writer who knew the exile.
views.E: The ban on intermarriage (23:12) is about worship, but it has been used to justify ethnic exclusion. Many readers set it beside Rahab and Ruth, who joined Israel.
views.J: Read as Joshua's ethical will. "The way of all the earth" (23:14) became a stock phrase for death. Holding on to God (devekut, from dabaq, 23:8) later became a central idea of Jewish piety, especially in Hasidism.
views.X: Christian readers hear in God's faithfulness to every word a pledge of the gospel's promises (2 Corinthians 1:20). The warning also stands behind New Testament calls to keep oneself from idols (1 John 5:21).

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:1–5; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Deuteronomy 31:1–29; 1 Samuel 12:1–25; 1 Kings 2:1–4; Judges 2:1–3; Numbers 33:55

settings.to: All Israel through its leaders: elders, heads, judges and officials
settings.when: "A long time later," when the LORD has given Israel rest
settings.why: Joshua reminds the leaders that the LORD fought for them. The remaining nations will be driven out too, if Israel holds to the book of the law of Moses. They must not speak the names of the nations' gods or marry them. Every good word God spoke has come true (23:14). Just as surely, if Israel breaks the covenant, the nations will become traps and thorns. Israel will vanish from the good land. The speech is a bridge to Judges.
views: Traditional readers take it as Joshua's own farewell, in the style of Moses' farewell in Deuteronomy.
Noth saw chapter 23 as one of the key speeches that mark the turns of the history. To exiles, the warning of losing the good land had already come true.

title: Choose Today: The Covenant at Shechem
sum: Joshua gathers all Israel at Shechem and speaks for God: from Terah's idols beyond the Euphrates to Abraham's call, the descent to Egypt, the exodus and the sea, Balaam's blessings, and the gift of a land they did not work for. Then he calls on them to choose whom they will serve, and declares that he and his family will serve the LORD.

The people choose the LORD. Joshua warns that they cannot serve so holy and jealous a God lightly; they insist. He makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of God's law, and sets up a great stone under the oak as a witness. The book ends with three burials: Joshua at Timnath-serah, Joseph's bones at Shechem, and Eleazar on his son's hill.
readings: Read as a covenant ceremony
History, demand, choice, witnesses, a written record, a warning: the chapter follows the pattern of an ancient treaty, with God as the great king and Israel as his people.
Read as a choice for every generation
The people at Shechem are told that they saw the sea with their own eyes. The story is meant to be retold, and the choice made again, by each generation that hears it.

views.H: A real covenant renewal at Shechem at the end of Joshua's life, in a form that matches Late Bronze Age treaties, with the long history of past kindness that later Assyrian treaties usually lack.
views.C: Many scholars think chapter 24 preserves an old tradition of a tribal covenant at Shechem, perhaps where groups who had not been in Egypt joined Israel. Others, such as Lothar Perlitt and John Van Seters, see a late composition from the age of Deuteronomy or after. Its history leaves out Sinai entirely. Gerhard von Rad took this as a sign that the story of exodus and conquest and the story of Sinai began as separate traditions, with this speech and Deuteronomy 26:5–9 as short historical creeds.
views.E: The covenant is a free choice, and Joshua warns against making it lightly. Readers also note that the gift of vineyards and olive trees "you never planted" (24:13) was someone else's loss.
views.J: The Passover Haggadah quotes 24:2–4: "In the beginning our ancestors served idols." The Talmud cites 24:26 in crediting Joshua with writing his book (Bava Batra 15a).
views.X: Joshua's "choose today" is one of the most quoted calls to decision in Christian preaching. Joseph's bones appear in Hebrews 11:22 and Acts 7:16, and Jesus speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well on Jacob's land near Shechem (John 4:5–6).

deep.b:
In the 1950s George Mendenhall compared the covenant passages of the Bible with Hittite treaties of the 1300s BC: a preamble naming the great king, a history of his kindness, demands of loyalty, provision for the text to be kept and read, divine witnesses, and blessings and curses. Joshua 24 fits closely: "The LORD, the God of Israel, says this" (24:2), the history (24:2–13), the demand (24:14–15), witnesses (24:22, 27), a written record (24:26) and warnings (24:19–20).

Kenneth Kitchen argued that the form points to an early date. The full pattern, with a long history of the great king's kindness and paired blessings and curses, belongs to the Late Bronze Age; the Assyrian treaties of the first millennium usually lack the history, and Joshua 24 has a long one. Dennis McCarthy granted the parallels but argued that Joshua 24 is a report of a covenant ceremony rather than the text of a treaty, and that treaty language lasted for centuries, so the form cannot date the chapter by itself. Lothar Perlitt and John Van Seters went further and read the chapter as a late composition, from the age of Deuteronomy or after, using covenant language to call a later Israel to decision.

echoes: Genesis 12:6–7; Genesis 35:1–4; Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19; Exodus 15:25; Deuteronomy 27:1–26; Deuteronomy 30:15–20; Judges 2:6–10; Judges 9:6; Acts 7:16; Hebrews 11:22; John 4:5–6

settings.to: All the tribes of Israel gathered at Shechem, with their elders, heads, judges and officials, standing before God
settings.when: at the end of Joshua's life
settings.why: Joshua leads a covenant renewal at Shechem. He retells the history in God's own voice and calls the people to choose whom they will serve. He declares, "I and my family will serve the LORD" (24:15). When the people choose the LORD, he warns that they cannot serve him lightly. He makes a covenant, writes it in the book of God's law, and sets up a great stone as a witness. For each generation that read it, the choice was set before them again.
views: Many scholars, following Noth and Mendenhall, think the chapter keeps memory of an old covenant at Shechem. It bound tribes, some of whom had not been in Egypt, into one people under the LORD. It follows the order of an ancient treaty.
Van Seters and others date it to the exile or later. On this view it sums up the whole story from Abraham to the land, to make readers choose again.
Traditional readers take it as Joshua's covenant with Israel, which he wrote down (24:26).

settings.to: All the tribes gathered at Shechem
settings.why: God speaks in the first person: "I took your forefather Abraham," I sent Moses, I brought you out, I gave you a land you did not work for. Joshua's hearers learn that everything they have is God's gift. They also learn that their ancestors once served other gods beyond the River. The history is the ground for the demand that follows.

settings.what: Choose today whom you will serve
settings.by: Joshua, and the people in answer
settings.to: All the tribes gathered at Shechem
settings.why: Joshua calls on the people to put away the gods their ancestors served beyond the River and in Egypt. Then they must choose. The people answer three times that they will serve the LORD. Joshua warns that the LORD is holy and jealous, and makes them witnesses against themselves (24:22). The back and forth makes the covenant the people's own free choice.

settings.what: The covenant and the witness stone
settings.why: Joshua makes a covenant for the people, sets out rules, and writes the words in the book of God's law. He sets up a large stone under the oak by the LORD's sanctuary. The stone "heard everything the LORD said" (24:27), and will witness if they deny their God. For later readers at Shechem, it was a visible reminder.

traditions.q: When Joshua tells Israel to choose whom they will serve, can people choose God on their own?
views: No one can turn to God without grace, but grace does not force the will. Moved by grace, a person freely agrees and cooperates, and can also refuse (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 5 and canon 4; Catechism 1993).

Before conversion the human will cannot choose God at all; the Holy Spirit alone turns the heart through the word (Formula of Concord, article 2; Luther, The Bondage of the Will). Yet those who are lost resist grace by their own fault, and Lutherans reject the idea that God chose anyone for damnation.

Fallen people have no power to choose God until he gives them new hearts (Westminster Confession 9.3). Joshua's call is the means God uses to bring his chosen people to a willing choice, but God's choice comes first (Canons of Dort, heads 3–4).

By prevenient grace, given to everyone, God restores enough freedom that every person can answer his call or refuse it (Articles of Religion 8). John Wesley argued that a call to choose would be empty if only some could answer (Predestination Calmly Considered).

Baptists are divided. The 1689 London Confession teaches Calvinist election, while the Baptist Faith and Message (article 5) affirms both God's choice and real human freedom without settling how they fit, and Southern Baptists hold both views.
